title: Can AI read the rules for greener buildings? We put it to work in 119 cities
gist: The World Bank used OpenAI's GPT-5.4 Mini to draft and Anthropic's Claude to review answers on building energy codes across 119 cities for its Building Green dataset, reaching about 80% accuracy in the first 21 economies at roughly US$27 per city and cutting per-jurisdiction research from 2-3 days to 4-6 hours of review.

insights.claim: For the World Bank's Building Green dataset, OpenAI's GPT-5.4 Mini drafted answers to 60 legal questions per city and Anthropic's Claude independently reviewed the legal basis, yielding about four in five correct answers in the first 21 economies reviewed.
insights.so_what: Real-world multi-model pipelines are delivering ~80% accuracy on legal research, viable with human review.
insights.quote: In the first 21 economies reviewed, about four in five answers were correct, at roughly US$27 per city in model costs and an estimated 1,500 researcher hours saved.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Testing and production of the World Bank's AI legal-research workflow from March to August 2026 cost about US$3,200 in OpenAI usage across 119 cities, roughly US$27 per city, despite each city run processing five to ten million words of legal text.
insights.so_what: Model inference cost is trivial versus labor for document-heavy research, implying large margin pressure on legal/regulatory data vendors.
insights.quote: came to about US$3,200 in OpenAI usage across all 119 cities, or roughly US$27 per city
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: A researcher previously needed two to three days per jurisdiction to draft 60 legally referenced answers, whereas reviewing AI-drafted answers now takes about four to six hours.
insights.so_what: Roughly 75-85% labor savings in regulatory research even with full human verification.
insights.quote: reviewing a city's AI-drafted answers now takes about four to six hours.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: AI accuracy on building-code questions reached 75% or higher in 18 of the first 21 economies and up to 95% in the best case, with nearly nine in ten yes/no and fixed-choice answers correct.
insights.so_what: AI performs best on structured, clearly answerable legal questions; open-ended tasks still need humans.
insights.quote: nearly nine in ten yes/no and fixed-choice answers were correct.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

themes.theme: AI failure modes and verification design

insights.claim: Early AI runs often reached a defensible substantive answer but cited the wrong legal instrument, undermining reproducibility.
insights.so_what: Citation accuracy, not answer plausibility, is the key gap for AI in legal and compliance workflows.
insights.quote: the AI often reached a defensible substantive answer but cited the wrong legal instrument.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Three recurring pitfalls for AI legal research were that detailed requirements often sit in ministerial regulations rather than the parent law, repealed local rules remain online, and the date of the legal instrument matters more than the webpage date.
insights.so_what: Practical rules for anyone building AI regulatory-intelligence products.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The World Bank's design routes every answer through an automated consistency check, a second-model review by Claude so the drafting model never grades its own work, and an analyst check against sources, publishing only answers passing all three.
insights.so_what: Cross-model verification is emerging as a best practice, supporting demand for multiple frontier model vendors.
insights.quote: so the drafting model never grades its own work
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The project produced a benchmark of 7,140 human-graded rows covering 60 questions across 119 cities, against which future automated verifiers can be tested.
insights.so_what: New public-sector benchmark for evaluating AI legal-research accuracy.
insights.quote: a benchmark of 7,140 human-graded rows, covering 60 questions across 119 cities.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The authors argue the main lesson is about design rather than models: send source-answerable questions to AI, keep experience-based questions with local experts, and rely on verification, citations and accepting 'insufficient evidence'.
insights.so_what: Value in AI deployments accrues to workflow design and verification, not raw model choice.
insights.quote: the main lesson is about design rather than models.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The authors say any dataset built from public records can be collected and checked using the same AI-plus-verification approach.
insights.so_what: Signals broad automation of public-records data collection across regulatory and indicator datasets.
insights.quote: any dataset built from public records can be collected, and checked, the same way.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Buildings and construction account for around 37% of global CO2 emissions, and energy codes are a main tool governments use to set efficiency standards for new construction.
insights.so_what: Building-code tightening is a major decarbonization lever affecting construction materials and efficiency markets.
insights.quote: Buildings and construction account for around 37 percent of global CO2 emissions
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Building Green's 2024 edition found that among 88 economies with a mandatory building energy code, just over a third had a functioning system for qualifying and overseeing compliance inspectors.
insights.so_what: Code-on-paper overstates real efficiency demand; enforcement gaps mute expected market effects.
insights.quote: just over a third had a functioning system for qualifying and overseeing the inspectors who check compliance.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The next Building Green edition, covering 119 cities in 110 economies, is due in spring 2027 and will pair legal requirements with local expert reports on enforcement in practice.
insights.so_what: Upcoming dataset will flag where green-building rules are actually enforced, useful for market sizing.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
